transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hey, Doc. Thanks for seeing me. Well, to be honest, it's... it's getting to be a real problem at work. I've been in construction since I got out of high school, worked my way up to site manager, so I know how to run a crew, you know? There's always a hundred moving parts on a site—subcontractors, material deliveries, weather delays, you name it. 

But what really brings me in today is... well, I'll sit down to run a morning safety briefing, or I'll be in the trailer doing a plan review with the architects. And I'm sitting there, trying so, so hard to just pay attention to the words on the page or the guy talking. I'm telling myself, "Focus, listen to this." But I swear, within minutes, my mind is completely gone. It's just off on three other job problems. I'll be staring right at the plans, but in my head, I'm stressing about whether the drywall guys are gonna show up, or if the city inspector signed off on the rough plumbing, or where the lumber drop is going to happen if it rains. 

And because my brain is a million miles away, I end up missing things. Important things I absolutely know I should have caught. I've been doing this for years, I shouldn't be missing basic structural specs or safety updates, but it's like I just can't keep my head in the room. And it's... it's starting to really scare me, honestly, because in my line of work, if you miss a safety detail, someone gets hurt, and I just can't seem to force myself to stay locked in on one thing.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn't an immediate problem to solve — like feeling anxious about things in general, not just specific work issues?

No, not really. I mean, it's not like I'm sitting around worrying about, you know, the state of the world or if the sky is falling or anything like that. It's really just the job. Like, I don't lay awake at night stressing about my health, or if I'm gonna get into a car accident, or, I don't know, general stuff like that. My wife, she's a worrier. She worries about the kids' grades, she worries about the mortgage rates, she worries if the dog is eating enough. But me? No, I don't really have that kind of anxiety. 

It's just... it's all the moving pieces at work. It's the concrete pour that might get rained out, or the electrician who's always two days behind schedule, or the permit office dragging their feet. That's the stuff that pulls my mind away when I'm trying to look at a blueprint. It's like my brain is just constantly running through the checklist of the site, trying to anticipate the next fire I have to put out. But if I'm, say, on vacation—which doesn't happen often, but when it does—or if I'm just hanging out on a Sunday watching the game, I'm not sitting there feeling anxious or worried about life in general. It's really just the sheer volume of stuff I have to manage on the site that hijacks my attention, you know? Not like a general panic about everything. Just... the job.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest or pleasure in most activities, even the ones you usually enjoy?

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't feel down or hopeless or anything like that. I'm actually a pretty upbeat guy, usually. I like my life, you know? I love my wife, I love my kids. We've got a good thing going. We try to get out on the boat on the weekends when the weather is nice, and I still really look forward to that. I mean, getting out on the water, feeling the sun, just kind of letting the engine roar for a bit... it's great. I still love doing that. And I still like firing up the grill on a Sunday, having the neighbors over, watching the game, having a couple of beers. All that stuff is still great. 

It's not that I'm losing interest in things, or feeling like life is pointless. It's just... it's just the frustration with my brain not doing what I want it to do when I'm at work. Like, I get mad at myself, sure. I get really aggravated when I realize I just spaced out during a whole conversation with the structural engineer. But it's not like a deep, dark sadness, you know? It's more like... like a really intense annoyance. Like, "Come on, man, get it together!" But as far as feeling depressed or hopeless? No, no, definitely not. I still enjoy my time off, I still enjoy my family, I still like my hobbies. It's just the work stuff that's driving me crazy because I can't seem to stay focused on the task at hand. But yeah, no, not depressed at all. Just... just really, really frustrated with myself.
